extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Renaissance humanism; scholars of Erasmus and rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of prescriptive rhetorical and editorial principles presented in a biographical/historical account of Erasmus (early 16th century humanist). Useful for understanding period pedagogy, rhetorical norms, and publishing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for brevity in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice for writers who value Spartan brevity: avoid prefaces and expressions of feeling, state your case simply and concisely, use arguments (at least the chief ones), and present them compactly so the argument lies almost in the wording itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ’He who likes the brevity of the Spartans will first of all avoid prefaces and expressions of feeling in the manner of the Athenians. He will state his case simply and concisely. He will use arguments,--not all but at least the chief ones, and will present these not in detail, but compactly, so that the argument shall be almost in the very wording, if anyone cares to work it out.’ Be sparing with amplifications, similes, examples; abstain from figures that make language merely 'rich, splendid, telling, elaborate, or attractive' when brevity is the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit of copia (abundant expression) when desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline for those who seek 'copia' (abundance of expression): expand material according to established rules to enrich and amplify discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ’On the other hand he who seeks for copia will desire to expand his material pretty nearly according to the rules I have laid down.’ (Implicit: there exist systematic techniques for amplification and enrichment to be applied when abundance is the objective.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation; balance brevity with aptness and warmth
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against affectation and the mechanical pursuit of few words; brevity must still convey the best possible content and retain warmth and vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ’Let each beware, lest through affectation he be carried over into the fault which lies nearest him. Let the lover of brevity see to it that he does not merely use few words, but that he says in the fewest words the very best thing he can.... For nothing is so conducive to brevity of style as aptness and elegance of words, and if we add simplicity, it will be easy to avoid obscurity... But here again we must look out that our speech does not grow cold through lack of all warmth of feeling. Therefore let the matter be so put before the eye that, of itself, it may silently take a certain hold upon the mind. Let all be sweetened with the Attic charm.’ Use apt, elegant, simple diction to avoid obscurity and emotional coldness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of model formulas and memorization for pupils (Copia verborum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical recommendation that students commit to memory the collections of ready-made phrases and formulas (Copia verborum) as a practical resource for classical schooling and rhetorical exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Copia verborum 'is filled with formulas for the expression of a multitude of ideas most likely to occur in the work of the classical pupil. This is pure hack-work, a mere mechanical enumeration, but likely to be of great use to those for whom it was intended. It would be an admirable thing if our own high-school pupils could be made to commit great parts of the copia verborum to memory.' (Practical guidance: learn set expressions to aid composition and teaching.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good printer/publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes and practices that make an edition or publishing house exemplary: scholarship, enlistment of learned collaborators, careful and elegant production, and an avoidance of profit-driven controversialism that would 'defile' good literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasmus praises Froben as a printer of the 'Aldus type'—a scholar who enlists scholars, issues editions in noble form, and keeps his house free from books of controversy 'lest the cause of good literature and learning should be defiled by any personal hostilities.' Practical markers of quality: accurate and elegant editions, collaboration with competent scholars (e.g., the Amerbach contribution), and editorial restraint regarding polemical content.
